intro: A Scottish seascape begins in the violas, cellos and bassoon: a six-note falling phrase, with the violins holding still above them. Mendelssohn turns that small phrase into the storms and long swells of The Hebrides.

relations.label: The lyrical phrase is restated
relations.basis: The lyrical second-subject group in the exposition reiterates its broad phrase over continuing accompanimental motion. Both measured spans lie in the D-major contrast identified near 120 s, not in the later recapitulation. CENS diagonal mean 0.927, sustained 19 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 27 s (cache/form/mendelssohn-hebrides.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Six notes below the violins
cues.text: Violas, cellos and first bassoon play a falling phrase in B minor. It starts after a quaver’s rest: F♯, D, C♯, D, B, F♯. Above it, the violins hold two quiet notes. The sea is already moving before anything rises to the surface.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, plate M.B. 8, p. 1, bars 1–2. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/74/IMSLP122244-PMLP05059-Mendelssohn_-_Die_Hebriden_FS_rsl.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A letter from the Hebrides
cues.text: On 7 August 1829, Mendelssohn writes to his family: “In order to make you understand how extraordinarily the Hebrides affected me, the following came into my mind there.” Beneath the words are twenty-one bars of music. His visit to Fingal’s Cave comes the next day.
cues.evidence: Mendelssohn’s letter to his family, 7 August 1829, reproduced and translated by Yale’s Art and Music in Britain exhibition. https://artandmusic.yale.edu/romantic-landscapes/mendelssohn-scotland/mendelssohn-gallery2-letter-his-family

cues.title: Cellos and bassoons sing
cues.text: The second tune opens out in D major, marked cantabile. Cellos and bassoons sing it together while the upper strings keep turning over their quick notes. The melody takes its time; the water beneath it never stills.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 9–10: cantabile theme in bassoons and cellos, with upper-string semiquavers.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: London hears the islands
cues.text: On 14 May 1832, The Hebrides reaches a London audience on a programme that also includes Mendelssohn’s overture to A Midsummer Night’s Dream. He goes back to the score after the concert and revises it again.
cues.evidence: Duncan Gillies, Portobello Orchestra programme note, records the London première, the accompanying overture and revision after the performance. https://www.theportobelloorchestra.co.uk/ProgrammeNotes/MendelssohnHebrides.php

cues.title: Winds call across the strings
cues.text: In the development, forceful wind calls break across quiet, rocking strings. The opening phrase passes through the violas and cellos, sometimes reduced to a few notes. The trumpets answer with a sharply repeated rhythm.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 17–19: wind accents above piano and pianissimo strings; trumpet figures marked marcato.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Turner’s steamship at Staffa
cues.text: Turner visits Staffa in 1831. In his painting Staffa, Fingal’s Cave, a steamship passes the island’s basalt cliffs: smoke and spray fill the air together. Mendelssohn has been there two years earlier.
cues.evidence: Yale Center for British Art, Staffa, Fingal’s Cave, c. 1831–32, B1978.43.14; the catalogue records Turner’s 1831 visit and the steamer. https://interactive.britishart.yale.edu/critique-of-reason/360/staffa-fingals-cave

cues.title: The low phrase comes back
cues.text: The falling phrase returns in B minor, with violas and cellos marked tranquillo. The violins keep moving above it. After the development’s wind calls and rushing scales, the low melody sounds close and familiar again.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 29–30: return of the opening phrase in lower strings, marked piano tranquillo.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A clarinet in B major
cues.text: The long second tune returns in B major. A clarinet sings it almost alone above held string chords, marked tranquillo assai — very calm. A second clarinet joins later in the phrase. The busy accompaniment of the first statement has fallen still.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 32: first clarinet, pianissimo and tranquillo assai, followed by second clarinet; sustained strings beneath.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Animato breaks the calm
cues.text: Animato, in tempo: the violins start running again, and the oboe picks out a short, detached phrase. The clarinet’s long song is over. B minor returns, and the quick notes spread through the orchestra.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 33 onwards: Animato in tempo, oboe staccato and renewed semiquavers in the violins.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A few notes remain
cues.text: The orchestra draws back. A clarinet recalls the falling phrase, the flute answers, and the strings pluck their last few notes. The ending leaves B minor hanging in a remarkably small space.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 42: clarinet recollection, flute phrase and final pianissimo pizzicato strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Cellos and bassoons take the long tune
transitions.from: A · The low strings’ falling phrase
transitions.to: B · Cellos and bassoons sing in D
transitions.how: The music reaches D major, B minor’s relative major. The double bass supplies a quiet D as cellos and bassoons begin the new melody, marked cantabile. Violins and violas continue their semiquavers, now sempre pp, always very soft.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 8–9, opening of the second subject.

transitions.title: Wind calls against rocking strings
transitions.from: C · Running strings, brass and timpani
transitions.to: Dev · Wind calls over quiet strings
transitions.how: The D-major closing music breaks off at rehearsal C. Horns and trumpets repeat their clipped rhythm as the strings fall to piano. The violins rock between notes while the low strings recall the falling phrase; wind chords interrupt at fortissimo, then immediately diminish.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 17–18, rehearsal C and the following wind and string exchanges.

transitions.title: The low strings recover the opening
transitions.from: Dev · Wind calls over quiet strings
transitions.to: A′ · The low phrase returns in B minor
transitions.how: The rushing scales subside, and the violas and cellos bring back the B-minor opening phrase, marked piano tranquillo. The double bass holds beneath them. Above, the violins continue rocking pairs of notes while the last wind calls fade.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 28–30: diminishing wind figures and the lower strings’ tranquillo return.

transitions.title: The clarinet finds B major
transitions.from: A′ · The low phrase returns in B minor
transitions.to: B′ · A clarinet sings in B major
transitions.how: The strings descend and grow quieter, then hold a B-major chord. Over their low B, the clarinet begins the second tune, tranquillo assai. D♯ takes the place of B minor’s D♮; the bassoons and cellos that first sang the tune now leave it to the clarinet.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, pp. 31–32: descent into the sustained B-major accompaniment and clarinet melody.

transitions.title: Animato sets the violins running
transitions.from: B′ · A clarinet sings in B major
transitions.how: The clarinets slow and diminish over the strings. Animato, in tempo restarts the violins’ semiquavers, with a detached oboe phrase above a held F♯ in the low strings. The harmony turns back towards B minor, and the bass soon begins to move again.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 33: un poco ritardando, then Animato in tempo, oboe staccato and F♯ in the low strings.

transitions.title: The clarinet has the last recollection
transitions.to: A″ · Clarinet, flute and plucked strings
transitions.how: The final B-minor passage contracts from full orchestra to a clarinet’s falling phrase and a brief flute answer. Strings change to pizzicato and pianissimo. Low B remains in the bass; the last plucked notes are followed by a written pause.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Rietz edition, p. 42, final bars.

source.title: Mendelssohn, The Hebrides (Fingal’s Cave), Op. 26, full score (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, Werke Serie 2, 1874, plate M.B. 8; Partitur-Bibliothek reprint)
source.locator: Opening, p. 1; D-major melody, pp. 9–10; development, pp. 17–29; returning themes, pp. 29–33; closing pages, pp. 33–42.

timeline.note: Violas, cellos and first bassoon play the falling phrase beneath two held violin notes.
Clarinets enter first, then oboes and flutes, holding notes above the moving lower strings.
Horns and trumpets join the swelling strings, with a timpani roll underneath.
The orchestra reaches fortissimo, then the violins’ running notes drop to pianissimo.
Cellos and bassoons sing the D-major tune above the upper strings’ rippling semiquavers.
Running strings meet short wind and brass figures, with timpani reinforcing the chords.
Wind and horn calls break across the strings’ quiet, rocking notes.
The woodwinds play short, detached notes above plucked strings.
Winds, brass and running strings gather at fortissimo above a timpani roll.
The wind phrases diminish; the lower strings recover their falling line, marked tranquillo.
Violas and cellos carry the returning B-minor phrase, with bassoon joining above the low strings.
A clarinet sings in B major over held pianissimo string chords; the second clarinet joins the phrase.
Animato: the violins run again beneath short, detached woodwind phrases.
Fast string figures drive through fortissimo wind and brass chords, with timpani beneath.
The clarinet recalls the falling phrase; a flute answers before the strings’ last plucked notes.

composer.epithet: At sixteen, he made eight string players sound like the most exhilarating orchestra in Europe.
facts: Ludwig Berger, piano; Carl Friedrich Zelter, composition
Düsseldorf music director, 1833–35; Leipzig Gewandhaus conductor from 1835
Married Cécile Jeanrenaud in 1837; five children; brother of Fanny Hensel
Leipzig Conservatoire, founded 1843; ten visits to Britain
composer.background:
In 1825, sixteen-year-old Felix Mendelssohn wrote a birthday present for his violin teacher, Eduard Rietz. It required four violins, two violas and two cellos, and gave Rietz a first-violin part that climbs out over the other seven players in long, buoyant arcs. The E♭ major Octet still sounds like someone discovering how much pleasure eight string instruments can make. Eleven years later, its composer played second viola in a public performance. Writing to Karl Klingemann on 31 January 1836, he admitted to “heart palpitations”.

He had been noisy from the start. In 1812, his sister Fanny wrote to friends in Hamburg: “Felix has a strong voice and sings all day.” He was born there on 3 February 1809; the family moved to Berlin two years later. His father Abraham was a banker, his grandfather Moses the Jewish philosopher. Abraham and Lea Mendelssohn had their children baptised as Christians in 1816 and used the additional surname Bartholdy. Fanny and Felix learnt piano with Ludwig Berger and composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter.
